clue.text: Try minimum of salt — enough

indicators.note: the minimum of a word is the least you can take, a single letter from its front

blocks.note: first letter of salt
ample means enough or plenty

explanation.surface: A cook tasting a dish suggests adding just a pinch of salt, which will be plenty.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash reads like a pause in a recipe; it simply separates the two parts of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To sample food or wine is to taste or test it, which is one everyday meaning of the verb try.

clue.text: Namely, senior who tells someone off?

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the noun 'one who tells someone off'

blocks.note: sc. is the abbreviation of Latin scilicet, meaning namely
a senior person is older

explanation.surface: Someone asks which person delivers the reprimands: the senior one, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: SC (scilicet) is the scholarly Latin abbreviation for namely, seen in footnotes; add OLDER to get SCOLDER.
explanation.definitionFit: A scolder is a person who rebukes or reprimands others, which is exactly telling them off.

clue.text: Female graduate, woman falling from grace

definitions.note: the answer is a female first name

blocks.note: MA is a Master of Arts, a graduate
Eve's eating of the apple brought the Fall in Genesis

explanation.surface: A woman with a degree suffers a scandalous fall from her position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Female' looks like an adjective for the graduate, but it is the definition: a girl's name. Maeve is an Irish name, borne by the legendary queen of Connacht.
explanation.definitionFit: Maeve is an Irish girl's given name, so it fits loosely as a typical example of a female person.

clue.text: Figure of speech unusual in TS Eliot

indicators.note: something unusual is out of its normal form, so the letters come in an abnormal order

blocks.note: the poet's name taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: A critic notes a rare rhetorical device that turns up in the poetry of T. S. Eliot.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet's name looks like the subject of literary criticism, but its seven letters are simply rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Litotes is a rhetorical device of understatement by negating the opposite, as in 'not bad' meaning good.

clue.text: Protection from sun on wild ground

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for sun
a heath is open uncultivated land

explanation.surface: A walker seeks shelter from the blazing sun out on open moorland.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests sunscreen or a hat; 'Protection' is a covering for a blade.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheath is a close-fitting cover that protects a knife or sword blade, so it is a kind of protective casing.

clue.text: Dither when entertaining a number in German city

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to take them in, so one part is held within another

blocks.note: taken as written
N stands for an unspecified number in maths
to hover is to waver or be undecided

explanation.surface: Someone hesitates while hosting a group of visitors in a German city.
explanation.walkthrough: N is the mathematician's symbol for any number. The outer word splits after its first letter to take in the A and N.
explanation.definitionFit: Hanover (Hannover in German) is the capital of Lower Saxony in northern Germany.

clue.text: Entrance a daughter on special journey?

blocks.note: taken as written
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter
a mission is a journey made for a particular purpose

explanation.surface: A father is captivated by his daughter as she sets off on an important trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrance' looks like the verb (to enchant, stressed on the second syllable), but it is the noun meaning entry. In a down clue, 'on' means placed above.
explanation.definitionFit: Admission is the act or right of entering a place, which is the noun sense of entrance.

clue.text: Greek in nasty situation, with energy half gone

indicators.note: when half of something has gone, only the remaining half of the letters is kept

blocks.note: hell is a very unpleasant situation
the whole word, written out, whose second half then goes

explanation.surface: A Greek is stuck in a horrible predicament, his energy half exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: Here the word energy is written out and then cut in half, rather than abbreviated to E as usual.
explanation.definitionFit: Hellene is the Greeks' own name for themselves, from Hellas, the ancient and modern name of Greece.

clue.text: Balance needed for climbs

blocks.note: first meaning: a weighing instrument
second meaning: goes up, as of a wall or a mountain

explanation.surface: A climber needs a good sense of balance to get up a rock face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balance' looks like the climber's poise, but it is the noun for a weighing device.
explanation.definitionFit: A pair of scales is a weighing balance, and someone who scales a cliff ascends or climbs it.

clue.text: Pets possibly calm — it's mad noise that is troublesome

indicators.note: something troublesome causes disorder, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement

blocks.note: fifteen letters taken together, ignoring the dash and apostrophe

explanation.surface: An owner pleads with noisy pets to quieten down because the racket is maddening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' marks the definition as an example: pets are one kind of the answer, not all of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Pets are tame creatures kept in the home, so they are an example of the broader class of tamed household beasts.

clue.text: Bring up a diver, one released before time

indicators.note: something released is let go, so that letter leaves the word

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the Roman numeral for one, which is removed
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Rescuers haul a diver up to the surface, freeing him just in time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bring up' suggests hauling to the surface, but here it means mention a topic. ADVERT as a verb is the formal word for referring to something.
explanation.definitionFit: To advert to a subject is to refer to it or mention it, the same as raising or broaching it in conversation.

clue.text: Showered in little room, is he beginning to dry?

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that single letter is used

blocks.note: lav is short for lavatory, a small room
taken as written
taken as written
first letter of dry

explanation.surface: Someone has had a shower in a cramped bathroom and wonders whether he is drying off yet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Showered' looks like washing under a shower, but it means given generously, as in showered with gifts. LAV is British slang for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: To lavish gifts or praise on someone is to bestow them in abundance, just as you might shower someone with presents.

clue.text: State provides rescue vessel, plus a new special group?

blocks.note: Noah's ark rescued the animals from the Flood
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new
the SAS is the Special Air Service, an elite British army regiment

explanation.surface: A government supplies a lifeboat and sets up a new task force.
explanation.walkthrough: The SAS (Special Air Service) is the British army's special forces regiment.
explanation.definitionFit: Arkansas is one of the fifty United States, in the south of the country, with Little Rock as its capital.

clue.text: Hit back? It could be somewhat unfair

indicators.note: 'could be' offers a possible new form, so the letters may be rearranged into another word

blocks.note: nine letters taken together, ignoring the question mark

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether retaliating with a blow might be considered unsporting.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark splits the fodder so the first two words read as a complete question. 'A bit thick' is a British idiom for something unreasonable or more than one should have to put up with.
explanation.definitionFit: In British idiom, calling treatment 'a bit thick' means it is rather unreasonable or excessive, so it serves for mildly unjust.

clue.text: Regretted keeping in, becoming spoilt

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold on to it, so one part is held inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
to rue is to regret

explanation.surface: A child kept indoors regretted it and turned into a sulky, pampered brat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoilt' suggests an indulged child; here it means damaged beyond repair.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ruined has been destroyed or wrecked, the damaged sense of spoilt rather than the pampered one.

clue.text: Fellow, one Bill, is seen as someone insane

blocks.note: a fellow is a man
the Roman numeral for one
ac is the abbreviation for account, a bill

explanation.surface: A man called Bill is regarded by everyone as a madman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name to go with 'Fellow', but it is an invoice, and AC is the abbreviation for account.
explanation.definitionFit: A maniac is a person who behaves wildly or is mentally deranged, the everyday word for a madman.

clue.text: Firm needs worker to join No 1 fellow

blocks.note: Adam was the first man in Genesis
the worker ant is a crossword staple for worker

explanation.surface: A business must recruit an employee to work alongside its top man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a company, but it is the adjective meaning unyielding.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone adamant refuses to be persuaded or change their mind, which is being firm or resolute.

clue.text: Hanging cloth needs one bit changed? Sure!

indicators.note: changing one bit means a single letter is swapped for another

blocks.note: a curtain is a cloth hung at a window

explanation.surface: A curtain needs a small alteration, and the tailor happily agrees.
explanation.walkthrough: The swap is unspecified: the U becomes an E, which the crossing letters or the definition confirm.
explanation.definitionFit: Being certain means having no doubt, which is the same as being sure of something.

clue.text: I start to fall asleep in feeble poem

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so these parts go within another

blocks.note: taken as written
to nod off is to begin to doze
pale can mean weak or feeble, as in a pale imitation

explanation.surface: A reader confesses to dozing off over a weak piece of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feeble poem' looks like one phrase describing the verse, but only the last word defines; feeble supplies the outer letters, as in a pale imitation.
explanation.definitionFit: A palinode is a poem in which the poet retracts something said in an earlier poem.

clue.text: Proposes job's outside India's capital

indicators.note: a capital is a head or upper-case letter, so only the opening letter is kept
to be outside something is to surround it, so one part wraps another

blocks.note: first letter of India
a job is a post, and the 's adds an S

explanation.surface: Someone suggests that a job abroad lies beyond the Indian capital, Delhi.
explanation.walkthrough: 'India's capital' looks like Delhi, but it is just the first letter. The outer word splits after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To posit a theory is to put it forward as a basis for argument, which is to propose or suggest it.

clue.text: Get Bible so translated for special interest groups

indicators.note: translating turns words into a different form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: seven letters taken together

explanation.surface: Campaigners want scripture rendered into another language for the benefit of particular pressure groups.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Translated' looks like a reference to Bible translation, which is a real cause; here it only rearranges letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Lobbies are organised pressure groups that try to influence lawmakers on behalf of a particular cause.

clue.text: Discussed action to restrict club

indicators.note: to restrict something is to hem it in, so one part is confined inside another

blocks.note: a bat is a club used in cricket or baseball
a deed is an act or action

explanation.surface: Members talked over a measure that would place limits on a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' looks like a society to be regulated, but it is a weapon or sporting bat.
explanation.definitionFit: To debate a matter is to argue it out formally, so debated means talked over or discussed.

clue.text: Celebrity hugged by fathers who are not nice people?

indicators.note: something hugged is held in the arms, so one part sits inside another

blocks.note: a star is a celebrity
dads are fathers

explanation.surface: A famous person is embraced by a crowd of dads, who turn out to be rather unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags understatement: the answer means worse than merely not nice.
explanation.definitionFit: Dastards are despicable cowards or villains, an old-fashioned term for thoroughly unpleasant individuals.

clue.text: Spotted copper catching criminal, finally

indicators.note: finally means at the very end, so only the closing letter is taken
to catch something is to hold it, so one part is held inside another

blocks.note: last letter of criminal
a bobby is a British police officer, named after Sir Robert Peel

explanation.surface: A police officer was seen apprehending a villain at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' looks like the verb seen, but it is the adjective covered in spots. Bobby is British slang for a policeman.
explanation.definitionFit: Something blobby is covered with blobs or splotches, so it is marked with spots, a playful word for dotted.

clue.text: The end — nothing very big

blocks.note: O looks like zero, nothing
mega is slang for huge

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict on a finale: it was no big deal.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes it read as a shrug at an anticlimax; it only separates definition from wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, so it stands for the final part, as in alpha and omega.

clue.text: Unsympathetic French queen associated with a 'pain free' situation!

definitions.text: Unsympathetic French queen associated with a 'pain free' situation!

blocks.note: surface reading: a state of comfort with no physical suffering
setter's reading: pain is French for bread, and the queen supposedly told breadless peasants to eat cake

explanation.surface: A heartless royal is linked, ironically, with a life free from suffering.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks hint at a foreign word: French pain means bread. The queen is said to have answered news of bread shortages with 'let them eat cake', though the story is probably apocryphal.
explanation.definitionFit: She was the queen consort of Louis XVI, guillotined in 1793, popularly remembered as callous towards the starving poor.

clue.text: Accepting cheers, the monarch

blocks.note: ta and cheers are both British informal thanks
a king is a monarch

explanation.surface: The king graciously acknowledges the applause of the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' looks like the crowd's applause, but it is British slang for thank you, as is TA.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking an offer or gift means receiving it willingly, which is the same as accepting it.

clue.text: Saintly northern ruler reversing some stupid laws, obviously

indicators.note: some of a phrase is only part of it, so the letters lie inside the run of words
to reverse is to go backwards, so the letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word, all of the second and the first of the third

explanation.surface: A holy king of the north overturns some obviously foolish legislation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obviously' does double duty: it rounds off the surface and supplies the final letter of the hidden run.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Oswald was a seventh-century Christian king of Northumbria in northern England, venerated as a saint and martyr.
